title: Amélie
synopsis: A shy waitress at the Two Windmills, a tin box of childhood treasures, and a man in a glass house who has been waiting for someone to listen.

nodes.text: The bathroom tile comes away under the heel of your hand and there's a hole behind it with a biscuit tin inside. In the tin: nine marbles, a cyclist on a tiny bike, a photograph of a boy squinting, and a plastic soldier missing one arm. Somebody hid this in 1955 and then grew up and got on with it.

choices.consequence: You decide on the bathroom floor at midnight to find the boy, with one rule attached: he must never learn who it was. You return it. It gets you to Telephone Booth, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You put the tin under your bed and take the lid off twice a night for a week, which is its own quiet kind of theft. You commit to keep it. The road to Telephone Booth is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The concierge, who has despised the tenant list since 1974, gives you the name in eleven seconds. You leave the tin in the phone booth on his corner, ring the phone from across the street, and watch a man of sixty in a good coat pick up, hear nothing, find the box, and sit down on the pavement of his own street.

choices.consequence: You stay behind the glass of a bar and watch a stranger be handed his childhood back. You are shaking. He is not. You watch. It gets you to Father's Garden Gnome, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You leave before the good part, out of politeness. You will think about the ending you didn't watch for the next eleven years. You commit to walk on. The road to Father's Garden Gnome is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Your father has built a shrine to your mother out of a garden ornament and a schedule. He gets up, he dusts, he sits. He owns a passport with no stamps in it and a plan to travel that begins the year after every year. In the garden, the gnome faces the house with the patience of a hostage.

choices.consequence: You steal a garden ornament from your own father and hand it to an air stewardess with an explanation she accepts far too easily. You commit to send the gnome traveling. The road to Glass Man is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You put the trowel back and drink the coffee he made wrong. Nothing changes, and it goes on not changing for three more years. You choose to leave it. By Glass Man, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Monsieur Dufayel, third floor, has bones that break if the day is uneven. He hasn't been outside since 1970. He paints the same Renoir every year — the dance under the trees, the striped jackets, light coming through the leaves in coins — and every year the girl at the centre of it comes out wrong. He watches your courtyard through a telescope.

choices.consequence: You knock with a jar of soup and stay ninety minutes. He talks about brushwork. Neither of you mentions the telescope, then or ever. You visit him. It gets you to Bal du Moulin de la Galette, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You go up the stairs quietly past his door. He hears you anyway; he hears everyone. He turns back to the girl's face. You commit to pass. The road to Bal du Moulin de la Galette is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Twenty years of copies stacked against the wall, each failing the same way: the girl with the glass, looking somewhere past the party. He can do the light through the leaves. He can do the wine. He cannot do a face that isn't in the room. You know that face. You've been avoiding it in shop windows for years.
nodes.sceneTitle: Bal du Moulin de la Galette

choices.consequence: You film the courtyard for him: a horse in a stairwell on somebody's television, ice cracking in a glass, a dog conducting a feud with a lamp post.

You bring a monograph with colour plates and he finds the right page in two seconds. He has owned that book since before you were born. You choose to bring a book. By Gina at the Cafe, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Gina works the tables beside you and reads bones — she'll take a regular's wrist and tell him something about his mother that lands. She is funny the way people are funny when they've decided not to be sad in public. Twice a week she looks at the door at eleven o'clock, and then stops looking at the door.

choices.consequence: You begin moving people around the cafe like furniture: a chair here, a remark dropped there. It works inside four days and nobody suspects a waitress.

You wipe the same table twice and let two lonely people go on failing to look at each other. It takes you nine days to change your mind. You commit to stay out of it. The road to The Hypochondriac is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Monsieur Vallee takes the corner table and his own pulse at the same time. Today it's a nerve in the leg, a sinus, and a heart that skips when it's humid. None of it is real; all of it is true. He describes each symptom to the room with genuine craftsmanship, and orders, as always, the same tea.

choices.consequence: You tell him the tea is contraindicated for precisely his condition. He believes you instantly, orders it anyway, and is thrilled to be living dangerously.

You take one symptom seriously for ninety seconds. He goes quiet, then talks about his sister for the first time in four years. You sympathize. It gets you to Joseph, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Joseph sits where he can see Gina and records her. Not photographs — a notebook, and a small tape recorder in his coat pocket. He has timed her laughs. He knows which customers get the real one. He will tell you, unprompted, that he isn't jealous, in the voice of a man reading a statement his lawyer wrote for him.

choices.consequence: You point him toward the tobacco counter and a woman with a lonely afternoon and a headache. Two problems, one table. You are not proud. You are pleased.

You ask what he'll do with the notebook once it's full. He has no answer, which is the first honest thing he has produced in months. You confront him. It gets you to Photobooth Album, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: A man drops an album on the metro stairs and doesn't come back for it. Inside: hundreds of passport photographs rescued from underneath the booths, torn, creased, thrown away by the people in them, no two faces the same, mounted with real care. On the last page, one man appears four times, four booths, four different years.

choices.consequence: You take it home and spend a night at your kitchen table with a magnifying glass, like a detective in a story about nothing at all. You choose to investigate. By Nino, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You tell yourself you'll hand it in Tuesday. You do not hand it in Tuesday. It sits on your table looking at you with four hundred faces. You borrow it. It gets you to Nino, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You find him at the Gare de l'Est with a screwdriver, opening the panel beneath a photo booth to sift the tray for what people threw away. He works at a ghost train and a sex shop. He collects laughs on tape and footprints in wet cement. He is, in short, a lunatic with a filing system, and you cannot breathe properly.

choices.consequence: You get within two metres and your legs make an executive decision without consulting you. You buy a ticket to somewhere you don't need to go.

You stand behind a pillar for forty minutes learning how he holds a screwdriver. This is what you have instead of a conversation. You commit to watch. The road to Lost Album Returned is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You make him work for it: a blue arrow chalked on a wall, a photograph taped to a lamp post, a payphone that rings at exactly the right second with a voice that is yours and doesn't sound like yours. He chases you across two arrondissements on a moped. He isn't annoyed. He's delighted, which is much worse.

choices.consequence: You hand him the album in a mask and a wig and run, which is either a game or a diagnosis, and you are not asking anyone which. You hide. It gets you to Tin Box Reunion, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You get four words out in a voice pitched somewhere up near the ceiling, then leave before he can produce a fifth. You speak. It gets you to Tin Box Reunion, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Bretodeau is in the phone booth with the lid off and the one-armed soldier in his fist. He is fifty-eight and weeping in a glass box on a Tuesday afternoon. Then he goes into the bar, orders a drink, and tells a total stranger about his daughter — who he hasn't telephoned in years, and who he telephones that night.

choices.consequence: You stand at the bar two metres from a man describing the best thing that ever happened to him, holding your own glass, saying nothing. You choose to stay nearby. By Grocer's Bullying, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You leave him to it and walk home the long way round. Something in your chest has been rearranged and there is nobody to tell. You commit to walk away. The road to Grocer's Bullying is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Collignon runs the produce stand, and runs Lucien, his apprentice, into the ground for sport — in front of customers, over an endive, in the voice people use on dogs. Lucien is slow, gentle, and carries groceries up four flights to a blind man. The whole street watches this happen twice a day and buys their leeks anyway.

choices.consequence: You take an impression of his door key in a bar of soap. You are now, technically, a burglar. You have never been happier. You switch his alarm clock. It gets you to Toothpaste Trick, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You buy your endives elsewhere and say nothing, which is the respectable option and sits in you like a swallowed coin. You choose to stay out of it. By Toothpaste Trick, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Over three weeks: his alarm clock advances by ninety minutes, his slippers shrink a size, the doorknob is swapped, the bulb over the stairs quietly dies, and his toothpaste becomes foot cream. You replace the photographs in his address book one at a time. By the end he is standing in his own kitchen at four in the morning holding a slipper, doubting his mind.

choices.consequence: You do the doorknob at two in the morning with a screwdriver borrowed from a man who does not yet know your name. You do it gleefully. It gets you to Glass Man's Letter, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You put the real toothpaste back and leave it. He is kinder to Lucien for six days, which may or may not be anything to do with you. You stop. It gets you to Glass Man's Letter, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Dufayel doesn't look up from the girl's face. He says bones mend and this doesn't, not if you keep spending yourself on other people's lives. Then he writes it down, folds it once, and puts it in your hand: one page about the man across the courtyard who ought to stop watching and go outside.

choices.consequence: You read a stranger's page aloud to Nino in a stairwell and it comes out sounding exactly like a confession, because that is what it is. You commit to read it aloud to Nino. The road to Father's Postcard is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You post it with no name on it, which is your solution to everything, then wait four days by a window like a woman in a painting. You commit to mail it. The road to Father's Postcard is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: A photograph arrives: your gnome at the foot of the Eiffel Tower, holding a tiny sign. Then Moscow, in snow. Then a pyramid, slightly out of focus, taken by an air stewardess with a demanding schedule. Your father props each one against the sugar bowl and studies it right through breakfast. After the fourth, he buys a suitcase.

choices.consequence: You frame the pyramid and set it in his hall, where he must walk past his own gnome having a considerably better year than he is. You commit to frame it. The road to Cafe Date is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You slip the photographs into his newspaper one at a time and never take a scrap of credit, which is becoming a medical condition. You commit to hide it. The road to Cafe Date is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The last clue works: Nino is at table four of the Two Windmills at five exactly, hands flat on the cloth, checking the door every eleven seconds. You are eight feet behind him holding a tray. You have arranged every single thing in this man's life for three weeks and you cannot currently arrange your own feet.

choices.consequence: You polish one glass for four minutes with your back to the room, listening to the sound of a man not being met. You watch from the back. It gets you to Cigarette Vendor, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You take the chair opposite and your whole body goes cold, and then he says hello, and it turns out to be a completely ordinary word. You choose to sit down. By Cigarette Vendor, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Georgette, who has seen everything there is to see from behind the tobacco counter, starts waving Nino over like a woman guiding in a plane. Gina is attempting something similar with her eyebrows. Every person employed here has understood the situation for a fortnight. You are in the kitchen doorway holding a tray, dissolving.

choices.consequence: You put a note under his saucer instead of a word in his ear. He reads it, smiles, leaves. The game buys you one more day. You send him a clue. It gets you to Moped to the Door, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You tell Georgette to stop, and clear his cup yourself. It is the bravest thing you have ever done and it lasts four seconds. You commit to stop the game. The road to Moped to the Door is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The doorbell goes at eight and it isn't a delivery, and there's no arrow left to chalk and no phone booth left to hide inside. Down in the street a moped leans against the kerb, still ticking as it cools. You are on the other side of six centimetres of wood, deciding what sort of person you are.

choices.consequence: You open the door with wet hands and no plan whatsoever, which for you constitutes a form of skydiving. You choose to open it. By Three Kisses, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You stand very still by the sink until the stairwell light clicks off. Then you open the door onto an empty landing and one folded note. You hide in the kitchen. It gets you to Three Kisses, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Cheek, cheek, the corner of the mouth — and then nothing anybody taught you. The plum tart sits on the counter going cold. Somewhere below, Dufayel is at his window with a telescope he is, on this one occasion, choosing not to use. The kitchen tap drips nine times. Neither of you says a single word.

choices.consequence: You move first, for the first time in your life, by about two centimetres. Two centimetres turns out to be the entire distance. You lean in. It gets you to Rooftops at Dawn, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You hold still and let him cross the last of it himself. It takes him nine seconds. You count every one of them. You choose to wait. By Rooftops at Dawn, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Morning over the zinc roofs: a man watering a plant he has never liked, a woman below pegging out a shirt, a cat in a window doing absolutely nothing with tremendous commitment. Somewhere down there a moped goes along a street with two people on it, and one of them is you, going too fast, holding on.

choices.consequence: You smile at the whole ridiculous city from the back of a moped, and the city, being Paris, takes full credit for everything. You smile back. It gets you to Three Times, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You watch the roofs going past instead and let the good thing happen without inspecting it, which for you is a first. You choose to look down. By Tin Box on a Shelf, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You ask him to stop at the third floor on the way back, because there's a man up there who should see this before the light changes. You commit to take the third path. The road to The Renoir Solved is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Two cheeks and a forehead in the morning, then a moped pulling off the kerb with a noise like an angry sewing machine. Your courtyard, which has heard forty years of shouting and one telescope being adjusted, now hears laughter at eight in the morning, twice a week, and once at three. Upstairs, Dufayel marks the date on the back of a canvas and gets on with the leaves.

You build a museum on the shelf above your bed: the tin, the marbles, a doorknob, four photographs, and one plastic soldier returned and then re-donated by a man who wanted it to live somewhere with company. People come from three streets over to look at other people's rubbish. You stand by the door and blush and explain each object in one perfect sentence, every time.

He finishes the girl's face in March, twenty-one years late, and it isn't her. It's you in the doorway of the Two Windmills, looking at nobody. He turns the easel around and watches you see it, then laughs, then cries, then offers you a glass of milk as though nothing whatsoever has occurred. You take the milk. It is cold and ordinary and you drink all of it.
